title: Hearing: How Ears Work
summary: How sound vibrations travel through the outer, middle, and inner ear, how hair cells in the cochlea send signals to the brain, and why loud noise can harm hearing for good.
poll: Listening to music very loudly is not a big problem for young people's ears.

versions.title: How We Hear
versions.text:
A bird sings. A door slams. You hear them. How?

Sound is a shake in the air. Things that make sound vibrate. They shake fast. The air shakes too. The shake moves to you.

Your outer ear is like a cup. It grabs the sound. The sound goes down a tube. At the end is the eardrum. It is thin, like skin on a drum. It shakes.

Next are three tiny bones. They are the smallest bones in your body. They pass the shake on.

Then the shake gets to the cochlea. It is shaped like a snail shell. It is full of fluid. Tiny hair cells sit in it. Some feel high sounds. Some feel low sounds. They send signals to a nerve. The nerve goes to the brain. Now you know what you hear!

Your inner ear helps with balance, too.

Loud sound can hurt the hair cells. They do not grow back. So keep the sound low. Your ears will thank you.

versions.title: How We Hear
versions.text:
A bird sings. A door slams. A friend calls your name. You hear each one. But how?

Sound is a shake that moves through the air. When something makes a sound, it starts to vibrate. That means it shakes back and forth very fast. The air near it shakes too. The shake moves all the way to you.

Your outer ear is shaped like a cup. It catches the sound. The sound goes down a short tube. At the end of the tube is the eardrum. It is thin and tight, like the skin on a drum. When sound hits it, it shakes.

Behind the eardrum are three tiny bones. They are the smallest bones in your body. They pass the shake along.

Next, the shake reaches the cochlea. It is shaped like a snail shell, and it is full of fluid. Tiny hair cells line it. Some sense high sounds, and some sense low sounds. They send signals down a nerve to your brain. Your brain tells you what the sound is.

Parts of your inner ear also help you keep your balance.

Very loud sound can harm the hair cells. They do not grow back. So turn the sound down and keep your ears safe.

versions.title: How Our Ears Hear
versions.text:
A bird sings in a tree. A door slams down the hall. A friend calls your name. You hear all of these sounds. But how do your ears do it?

Every sound starts with a shake. When something makes a sound, it begins to vibrate. It moves back and forth very fast. This makes the air around it shake too. The shaking air travels in waves until it reaches you.

Your outer ear is shaped like a cup. It catches sound and sends it down a short tube called the ear canal. At the end of the canal is the eardrum. It is a thin, tight piece of skin, like the top of a drum. When sound waves hit it, it shakes.

Behind the eardrum are three tiny bones. They are the smallest bones in your whole body. They pass the shaking along and make it stronger.

Next, the shaking reaches the cochlea. This part looks like a snail shell, and it is full of fluid. Thousands of tiny hair cells line the inside. Some hair cells sense high sounds, and others sense low sounds. They turn the shaking into signals. A nerve carries the signals to your brain. Then your brain tells you what you heard.

Your inner ear has another job, too. It helps you keep your balance.

Very loud sounds can hurt the hair cells. Once they are damaged, they do not grow back. That is why you should keep the volume low.

A bird sings in a tree, a door slams down the hall, and a friend calls your name. You hear all of these sounds in less than a second. How do your ears do it?

Every sound starts with a vibration. When something makes a sound, it begins to vibrate, which means it moves back and forth very fast. This makes the air around it shake too. The shaking air travels in waves, like ripples on a pond, until it reaches you.

Your outer ear is shaped like a cup, so it catches sound and sends it into a short tube called the ear canal. At the end of the canal is the eardrum, a thin, tight piece of skin like the top of a drum. When sound waves hit it, the eardrum shakes.

Behind the eardrum are three tiny bones called the hammer, the anvil, and the stirrup. They are the smallest bones in the human body. They pass the shaking along and make it stronger.

Next, the shaking reaches the cochlea, a part that is shaped like a snail shell and full of fluid. Thousands of tiny hair cells line the inside. Some sense high sounds, while others sense low sounds. The hair cells turn the shaking into signals. A nerve carries the signals to your brain, and then your brain tells you what you heard.

Your inner ear has another job, too, because it helps you keep your balance when you run or spin.

Very loud sounds can hurt the hair cells. Once they are damaged, they never grow back. That is why it is smart to keep the volume low.

versions.title: Hearing: How Ears Work
versions.text:
A bird sings in a tree, a door slams down the hall, and a friend calls your name. You hear every one of these sounds in less than a second. How do your ears manage this?

Every sound begins with a vibration. When an object makes a sound, it starts to vibrate, which means it moves back and forth very quickly. This movement makes the air around it vibrate too. The moving air travels outward in waves, a little like ripples spreading across a pond, until it reaches your ears.

Your outer ear is shaped like a cup, so it catches sound waves and guides them into a short tube called the ear canal. At the end of the canal sits the eardrum, a thin, tight piece of skin. When sound waves strike it, the eardrum begins to shake.

Behind the eardrum are three tiny bones called the hammer, the anvil, and the stirrup. They are the smallest bones in the human body. Together they pass the vibration along and make it stronger.

Next, the vibration reaches the cochlea, a part shaped like a snail shell and filled with fluid. Thousands of tiny hair cells line the inside. Some respond to high sounds, while others respond to low sounds. The hair cells change the vibration into signals, and a nerve carries those signals to the brain. Only then do you know what you heard.

The inner ear also helps you keep your balance when you walk, run, or spin. And because you have two ears, your brain can tell which direction a sound is coming from.

Very loud noise can damage the hair cells, and they do not grow back. Keeping the volume low protects your hearing for life.

versions.title: Hearing: How Ears Work
versions.text:
A bird sings in a palm tree, a door slams down the hall, and a friend calls your name from across the playground. Your ears notice each of these sounds almost instantly. Behind this simple experience is a remarkable chain of events.

Every sound begins with vibration. When an object makes a sound, it moves back and forth very rapidly, and this movement pushes on the air around it. The air carries the vibration outward in waves, much like ripples spreading across a pond, until the waves reach your ears.

The outer ear, the curved part you can see, works like a funnel. It collects sound waves and directs them into the ear canal, a short tunnel that leads inside your head. At the end of the canal is the eardrum, a thin, tightly stretched piece of skin. When sound waves strike it, the eardrum vibrates.

Behind the eardrum lie three tiny bones known as the hammer, the anvil, and the stirrup. They are the smallest bones in the human body, and together they pass the vibration along while making it stronger.

The vibration then enters the cochlea, a coiled tube shaped like a snail shell and filled with fluid. Thousands of tiny hair cells line the cochlea. Some respond to high sounds, while others respond to low ones. These cells change the vibration into electrical signals, which travel along a nerve to the brain. Only when the signals arrive does the brain recognize the sound as a song, a slam, or a voice.

Other parts of the inner ear help you keep your balance. Because you have two ears, your brain can also work out which direction a sound comes from.

Loud noise can damage the delicate hair cells, and they never grow back. For that reason, it is wise to keep headphones at a low volume.

versions.title: Hearing: How Ears Work
versions.text:
A bird sings in a palm tree, a door slams somewhere down the corridor, and a friend calls your name from across the playground, and your ears register each of these sounds almost instantaneously. Behind this ordinary experience lies a remarkable sequence of mechanical and electrical events that transforms invisible movements of air into meaningful information.

Every sound originates as a vibration. When an object produces a sound, it oscillates back and forth extremely rapidly, alternately compressing and stretching the air molecules surrounding it. The air transmits this vibration outward as pressure waves, comparable to ripples spreading across a pond, until the waves eventually reach a listener.

The outer ear, the curved, cartilage-supported structure visible on the side of the head, operates like a funnel that gathers sound waves and channels them into the ear canal, a short passage leading inward. Glands along the canal produce earwax, a sticky substance that traps dust and protects the delicate skin, which is why doctors discourage poking inside with cotton swabs. At the far end of the canal sits the eardrum, a thin, tightly stretched membrane that vibrates whenever sound waves strike it.

Behind the eardrum, in an air-filled chamber called the middle ear, are three minute bones known as the hammer, the anvil, and the stirrup. They are the smallest bones in the human body, and together they transmit the vibration inward while amplifying it considerably.

The vibration next travels into the cochlea, a coiled, fluid-filled tube resembling a snail shell. Thousands of microscopic hair cells line the cochlea, and different groups respond to different frequencies, some to high-pitched sounds and others to low-pitched ones. These specialized cells convert the mechanical vibration into electrical signals, which travel along the auditory nerve to the brain. Only when the signals arrive does the brain interpret the sound as birdsong, a slamming door, or a familiar voice.

Neighboring structures in the inner ear, which also contain fluid, help the body maintain its balance. Furthermore, because humans possess two ears, the brain compares the timing and loudness of the sounds reaching each one and thereby calculates the direction from which a noise originates.

Excessively loud noise can permanently damage the delicate hair cells, because the human body is unable to replace them once they are destroyed. For that reason, audiologists recommend keeping headphones at a moderate volume, wearing protection near powerful machinery, and allowing the ears to recover after noisy events.

Glands along the canal secrete earwax, a sticky substance that captures dust and protects the sensitive skin, which explains why physicians discourage people from inserting cotton swabs. At the innermost end of the canal sits the eardrum, a thin, tightly stretched membrane that vibrates whenever sound waves strike it.

The vibration subsequently travels into the cochlea, a coiled, fluid-filled tube resembling a snail shell. Only when the signals arrive does the brain interpret the sound as birdsong, a slamming door, or a familiar voice.

Neighboring structures in the inner ear, which also contain fluid, enable the body to maintain its balance and orientation. Furthermore, because humans possess two ears, the brain compares the timing and intensity of the sounds reaching each one and thereby calculates the direction from which a particular noise originates.

Excessively loud noise can permanently damage the delicate hair cells, because the human body is incapable of regenerating them once they are destroyed. LOW.prompt: Explain the path a sound takes from the air to your brain. Use at least three parts of the ear in the right order.
checklist: I named at least three parts of the ear.
I put the parts in the right order.

LOW.modelAnswer: First, a sound makes the air vibrate, and those vibrations travel into my outer ear. Next, the vibrations hit my eardrum, which shakes, and three tiny bones pass the shake along into my cochlea. Inside the cochlea, the vibration turns into a signal that travels along a nerve all the way to my brain, so I can finally hear the sound.

MID.prompt: Imagine you are explaining hearing to a younger student. Describe what happens after a sound wave reaches the eardrum, and give one way to protect your ears.

I gave one way to protect hearing and explained why it helps.

MID.modelAnswer: After a sound wave reaches the eardrum, it makes the eardrum vibrate, and three tiny bones pass that vibration along and make it even stronger. The vibration then travels into the cochlea, where tiny hair cells turn it into an electrical signal. That signal travels along a nerve to the brain, which finally recognizes the sound. One way to protect your ears is to keep headphones at a lower volume, because loud noise can damage the hair cells, and they never grow back.

keyWords.example: The auditory test showed that his hearing was normal.

keyWords.definition: a thin, flexible layer of tissue that covers or separates parts of the body
keyWords.example: A thin membrane covers the inside of an egg shell.
The doctor said to drink plenty of fluid on hot days.

keyWords.definition: how many times a wave vibrates each second; it decides whether a sound is high-pitched or low-pitched
keyWords.example: A whistle has a much higher frequency than a drum.

keyWords.definition: lasting forever or for a very long time; not able to be undone
keyWords.example: The marker left a permanent stain on my shirt.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Sound waves travel faster through fluid than through air.
Hearing depends on a chain of structures that turn air vibrations into signals the brain interprets, and this system can be permanently harmed.
The middle ear is the most important part of hearing.
Audiologists are the only people who understand how the ear works, so students should not try to learn about it.
questions.why: The article traces each stage from vibration to brain and closes by explaining permanent damage from loud noise.

wrong.A: The article does not compare the speed of sound in fluid and air.
wrong.C: The article treats every part as necessary; it does not rank the middle ear first.
wrong.D: Audiologists are mentioned only for their advice.

questions.stem: According to the article, what do the hair cells in the cochlea do?
options: They secrete earwax to trap dust
They amplify vibrations in the middle ear
They convert mechanical vibration into electrical signals
They stretch the eardrum tight
questions.why: The article says these specialized cells convert the mechanical vibration into electrical signals.

wrong.A: Glands in the ear canal produce earwax.
wrong.B: The three small bones amplify the vibration.
wrong.D: Nothing in the article says hair cells affect the eardrum.

questions.stem: Which sequence is correct?
options: Ear canal, eardrum, three small bones, cochlea, auditory nerve
Eardrum, ear canal, cochlea, three small bones, auditory nerve
Cochlea, eardrum, ear canal, auditory nerve, three small bones
Auditory nerve, cochlea, three small bones, eardrum, ear canal
questions.why: Sound passes down the ear canal to the eardrum, then the bones, then the cochlea, and the signals go along the auditory nerve.

wrong.B: The ear canal comes before the eardrum, and the bones come before the cochlea.
wrong.C: The cochlea is near the end of the path, not the start.
wrong.D: This is the path in reverse.

questions.stem: Why do doctors discourage people from inserting cotton swabs into their ears?
options: Swabs block the auditory nerve
Earwax is harmful, so it should be pushed deep inside the ear canal
Swabs make the hair cells grow back
Earwax already traps dust and protects the delicate skin
questions.why: The article explains that earwax protects the canal, which is why poking inside is discouraged.

wrong.A: The auditory nerve is deep inside and is not mentioned with swabs.
wrong.B: The article says earwax protects the ear; it does not call it harmful.
wrong.C: The article says hair cells cannot regrow.

questions.stem: Based on the article, what can you infer about a person who is unable to hear high-pitched sounds but still hears low ones?
options: The person's ear canal is completely blocked
The hair cells that respond to high frequencies may be damaged
The person has lost the three small bones
The person's sense of balance must also be lost completely and forever
questions.why: Since different hair cells respond to different frequencies, losing only high sounds suggests damage to the cells for high frequencies.

wrong.A: A fully blocked canal would affect all sounds, not just high ones.
wrong.C: Without the bones, both high and low sounds would be affected.
wrong.D: Balance comes from neighboring structures; losing some hearing does not mean losing balance.

questions.stem: In the article, the eardrum is called "a thin, tightly stretched membrane." Which word could best replace "membrane" here?
options: bone
liquid
nerve
sheet of tissue
questions.why: A membrane is a thin, flexible layer, so "sheet of tissue" fits the description of the eardrum.

wrong.A: A bone is hard, not thin and stretched.
wrong.B: The eardrum is solid tissue, not a liquid.
wrong.C: A nerve carries signals; the eardrum vibrates.

questions.stem: How does having two ears help the brain, according to the article?
options: It compares the timing and loudness of sounds at each ear to find their direction
It doubles the number of bones that amplify sound
It lets one ear rest while the other one hears
It allows the brain to repair damaged hair cells
questions.why: The article says the brain compares the timing and loudness of sounds reaching each ear to calculate direction.

wrong.B: Each ear has its own bones, but the article does not link this to direction.
wrong.C: The article does not say ears take turns resting.
wrong.D: Hair cells cannot be repaired, according to the article.

questions.stem: Why does the author open the article with a bird, a door, and a friend's voice?
options: To argue that birdsong is the most pleasant sound that people can hear each day
To show that the ear works best outdoors
To connect familiar sounds to the hidden process that lets us hear them
To explain how doors and birds make sounds
questions.why: The everyday examples show how ordinary hearing seems, before the author reveals the remarkable process behind it.

wrong.A: The author does not compare how pleasant sounds are.
wrong.B: The article does not say the ear works best outdoors.
wrong.D: The article is about how we hear sounds, not how birds and doors make them.

HIGH.prompt: The article states that hair-cell damage is permanent. Write a short paragraph arguing for one rule your school could follow to protect students' hearing, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I stated a clear rule and explained how it protects hearing.
I used at least two facts from the article as evidence.
I used precise vocabulary, including at least two key words.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think our school should set a rule limiting headphone volume during breaks, because the article explains that hair-cell damage from loud noise is permanent and the delicate cells never grow back once they are harmed. These hair cells line the fluid-filled cochlea and are essential to the auditory system, since they convert vibrations into the signals the brain uses to hear. Different hair cells respond to different frequencies, so losing them to loud noise could permanently weaken a student's ability to hear certain sounds for the rest of their life. A simple volume rule would protect this fragile, irreplaceable part of the ear before any damage can happen.
